overview: The atlas keeps the name “Nan Chao” on maps from 800 to 1279, but history refuses to fit that label. Nanzhao was a powerful kingdom centered around Erhai Lake and present-day Dali. Its rulers balanced Tang China and Tibet, fought far beyond their capital, sponsored Buddhism, moved books and crafts, and depended on farmers who shaped water into rice fields. Then the Nanzhao ruling house fell in 902. Short-lived regimes followed, and the different Dali kingdom began in 937. Mongol armies conquered Dali in 1253, yet the atlas still carries the older name for another twenty-six years. The map geometry has problems too: its 800 and 900 shapes miss the actual capital region and stretch far southeast; only the 1000 shape shifts back over Dali. This card follows the atlas interval while clearly changing political chapters. Along the way, inscriptions, excavated kilns, painted scrolls, family names and even music played on leaves reveal lives that no single kingdom label can hold.

periods.title: A kingdom between Tang and Tibet
periods.summary: Nanzhao ruled around Erhai as a major regional power, changing alliances and using warfare, diplomacy and mountain routes to bargain with two much larger neighbors.

periods.title: Chengdu raid and captured skills
periods.summary: Nanzhao forces raided Chengdu in 829 and carried away artisans and silk workers. Elite students had also learned there, so knowledge crossed the frontier through both study and coercion.

periods.title: Annan war and Buddhist royal power
periods.summary: Nanzhao occupied Annan from 863 to 866 before Tang forces returned. By 899 its court also used Buddhist stories and images to give kingship a sacred past.

periods.title: Nanzhao ends; short regimes follow
periods.summary: The ruling house was overthrown in 902. Changhe and other brief regimes succeeded it, carrying some royal Buddhist practices forward before Duan Siping founded Dali in 937.

periods.title: Dali replaces Nanzhao
periods.summary: The Duan house founded a new kingdom at Dali. A brief Dazhong regime interrupted Duan rule from 1094 to 1096, after which the restored polity is often called Later Dali.

periods.title: Later Dali: clans, books and Buddhist rule
periods.summary: Duan monarchs governed through alliances with powerful families and local leaders. Imported texts, religious institutions and trade helped connect the court to several surrounding regions.

periods.title: Mongol conquest and institutional afterlife
periods.summary: Mongol armies defeated Dali in 1253, long before the atlas label ends. Conquerors reused local elites and institutions while turning the former kingdom into a new imperial frontier.

items.text: At 800 the exact id is one 20-position polygon, but Taihe, Dali and Weishan all test outside it. Kunming and faraway Luang Prabang test inside. The imported shape therefore misses Nanzhao’s Erhai capital core and reaches much too far southeast; it is a display error, not a historical frontier.

The 900 layer repeats almost the same problem in 21 positions: Taihe and Weishan remain outside while Kunming and Luang Prabang remain inside. This snapshot stands only two years before Nanzhao’s historical end, so its misplaced outline cannot rescue the label by representing an earlier heartland.

By 1000 the atlas shape jumps west. Its 12-position polygon now includes Dali, Weishan and Kunming but leaves Luang Prabang outside. The geography is closer to the political center, yet the name is now anachronistic: the Duan family’s Dali kingdom, founded in 937, ruled this core.

The 1100 and 1200 polygons keep nearly the same west-shifted footprint, with 12 and 14 positions respectively. Both include Dali and Kunming. These layers can help locate successor-era history, but calling that history “Nan Chao” hides the Later Dali kingdom and its own rulers.

The separate nan-zhao id appears at 700, while nan-chao begins at 800 and disappears at 1279. Those seams belong to the atlas database. This card does not alias the two ids, and 1279 cannot be a local fall date: Nanzhao ended in 902 and Dali fell in 1253.

Nanzhao’s kings maneuvered between Tang China and the Tibetan empire. Alliances changed when rulers judged that a neighbor had become dangerous or useful. That was statecraft in a crowded borderland, not proof that Nanzhao permanently belonged to either empire. Armies, marriage ties, titles and envoys all shaped the contest.

In 829 Nanzhao forces attacked Chengdu and carried off prisoners, including artisans and silk weavers. The raid expanded the kingdom’s access to valuable skills through violence. A beautiful textile made afterward might preserve technical knowledge while concealing the forced journey of the worker who knew how to weave it.

Nanzhao forces took Annan, centered in northern Vietnam, in 863 and held it until Tang armies recovered the region in 866. A garrison of about 20,000 shows the scale of occupation. The episode also warns against treating every place touched by an army as a permanent part of one kingdom.

Military success rested on more than mounted warriors. Officials collected supplies, craftspeople repaired equipment, farmers produced grain and routes carried messages through difficult terrain. The surviving sources celebrate rulers and campaigns far more often than these workers, so reconstructing war means noticing the labor that court narratives leave mostly unnamed.

The 766 Dehua Stele gives Nanzhao’s own court explanation for breaking with Tang and aligning with Tibet. Much of the stone later became difficult to read, while older written copies preserved more. It is a political argument from one side, valuable precisely because readers can compare its purpose with its information.

Nanzhao’s ruling house was overthrown in 902. This is the card’s central chronology correction: almost four-fifths of the atlas interval comes after the historical kingdom had ended. Families, farms, workshops and temples did not vanish, but the state called Nanzhao no longer governed them.

Changhe ruled from 903 to 927, followed by two more short regimes before Dali began in 937. Changhe rulers still used Buddhist ideas of kingship, showing continuity without turning them into Nanzhao kings. A successor may inherit ceremonies, scribes and sacred stories while remaining a different government.

Duan Siping founded the Dali kingdom in 937. In 1094 Gao Shengtai replaced Duan rule with the brief Dazhong regime; Duan rule returned in 1096. Historians therefore distinguish Earlier and Later Dali. Even the successor state has a seam that the smooth atlas label does not show.

Later Dali government joined Duan monarchs with powerful Gao, Yang and Dong families and with leaders on the kingdom’s edges. Some units were militarized and semi-autonomous. This was layered rule built through personal and clan alliances, so a map outline cannot tell us how tightly any distant community was controlled.

Mongol armies defeated Dali in 1253. Yuan rulers then used local personnel and institutions rather than erasing them, while the atlas waits until 1279 to drop “nan-chao.” The later date matches a broad imperial milestone better than local succession. Conquest changed the framework of power and preserved selected pieces of it.

sections.title: Water, fields and food on the table

items.text: Around Erhai, farmers expanded wet-rice cultivation with terraces, channels and embankments. Waterworks supported dense settlements and the capitals at Taihe and Yangjumie. They were achievements made by planners and many laborers, not magic gifts from kings, even when royal inscriptions claimed the credit.

The 766 Dehua inscription praises flood control, rice, millet, orchards, household mulberry plots and grain stored for nine years. It predates this card by 34 years but belongs to the same Nanzhao court. Its sweeping abundance is royal rhetoric, not proof that every family always had enough food.

Fan Chuo says paddy fields produced one rice harvest, then farmers sowed barley after the rice and harvested it in spring. The sequence is a valuable clue to intensive cropping. It describes particular fields in a ninth-century gazetteer, so it cannot be assumed for every elevation or community in Yunnan.

Fan Chuo reports that an eleventh-lunar-month gathering involved brewing drink, preparing cattle and sheep, and entertaining relatives and neighbors. That is a vivid meal scene, but it comes from a ninth-century outsider and a special gathering. It cannot stand for breakfast, lunch and dinner in every household all year.

Fan Chuo describes salt wells whose output supplied food and says officials controlled access to at least one especially valued well. Salt makes meals taste different and helps preserve food, but a gazetteer’s attention to production and taxation tells us little about how much each household could afford.

Fan Chuo describes noblewomen in silk skirts and jackets with brocade, pearls, gold, shells and amber. He separately mentions female servants in skirts and felt coverings. The contrast reveals household rank more clearly than it reveals every woman’s routine, because an elite-focused outsider noticed display and difference.

The same account says young men made evening music with gourd instruments or even leaves during courtship. A leaf could become a tiny instrument without a workshop. This charming report belongs to a selected ninth-century setting; it does not prove that every family approved the same matches or courtship rules.

A later Dali Buddhist handscroll names married donors Chen Qing and his wife Lian. Their joint appearance shows a household sponsoring religious art, while the carefully recorded names let us glimpse real people behind the image. Patronage could express devotion, status, family memory or several of these at once.

The same scroll links a father named Chen Qing with a son named Qingfu by repeating Qing. Museum documentation identifies this as a Yunnanese genealogical naming practice. One family’s names cannot define the whole population, but they preserve a small, unusually personal clue about kinship and remembrance.

Fan Chuo’s feast passage brings relatives and neighbors together as guests, which shows that social life reached beyond one nuclear household. Yet a festival visit cannot tell us who normally shared a roof, how children divided work or how inheritance operated. Those family details remain largely unrecorded.

sections.title: Learning, books and an honest language sample

items.text: Elite Nanzhao young men studied literacy and numeracy in Chengdu. This is evidence for selected male students crossing a political border, not a kingdom-wide school system. The sources reviewed do not establish universal childhood education, village classroom routines or a comparable curriculum for girls, so those gaps should stay visible.

Dali obtained Sinitic books through the horse trade and used them to train officials. A 1173 list includes classics, histories, rhyming guides, Buddhist sutras and works on medicine. That collection shows what educated elites valued; it does not tell us how many copies existed or who beyond court circles could read them.

The short sample 厄塞流潦 means “blocking the floodwaters.” It comes from the transmitted Chinese text of Nanzhao’s 766 Dehua inscription. The phrase is directly tied to the Nanzhao court, though it falls just before this card’s 800 opening and survives through copying as well as the weathered stone.

This sample is Literary Chinese used for an official monument, an external prestige language for government writing. It is not a phonetic record of everyday speech and should not be presented as a sentence in modern Bai, Yi or another living language. The honest label matters more than pretending the missing voice survives.

Dali manuscripts and paintings could combine Chinese writing with Sanskrit Buddhist formulas. Zhang Shengwen’s late twelfth-century scroll includes Chinese and Sanskrit pillars among hundreds of figures. This multilingual page-world reflects court religion and learned exchange, while leaving most people’s spoken words unrecorded.

At Wuzhishan near Taihe, excavators uncovered courtyards with main halls, side corridors and porches. Buddhist images and miniature pagodas helped identify a temple complex. The site turns court religion into a built place where stone foundations, roof tiles, movement paths and repeated repairs mattered every day.

Kilns east of the temple held firing supports, spacers, molds and imperfect glazed pottery. Rejects are archaeological treasure because they preserve production mistakes that finished objects hide. The evidence places practical manufacturing beside sacred buildings, where potters, carriers and builders contributed to an impressive religious landscape.

A tile from Building One bears the Chinese characters 官家舍利, interpreted as “royal relics.” Excavation director Zhu Zhonghua proposed that the hall may have enshrined relics linked with the ruling house. The interpretation is plausible but still a proposal; no named king was found neatly labelled inside.

The 899 Illustrated History of Nanzhao tells how Acuoye Guanyin introduced Buddhism and granted the first kings a sacred mandate. The story helped the late court explain why its dynasty deserved to rule. It is an achievement of political storytelling and religious art, not an eyewitness report from Nanzhao’s beginnings.

A Dali sculpture at the Metropolitan Museum gives Avalokiteshvara twenty-four arms holding objects such as the sun, moon, bell and vajra. Cast in gilt arsenical bronze in the eleventh or twelfth century, it joins technical skill with a protective tantric form. Each arm turns theology into visible design.

sections.title: Trade routes carried things and ideas

items.text: Yunnan’s horse trade joined the region to neighboring courts and markets. Exchange was political as well as commercial: rulers wanted strong animals and dependable partners, while handlers needed fodder, tack and safe stages. A caravan’s success depended on practical knowledge that elite accounts rarely bother to name.

Silver left Yunnan and cowries entered its monetary life, linking mountain communities with distant markets. These flows did not make everyone a wealthy merchant. Miners, pack-animal handlers, brokers, officials and customers met the same network from different positions, and surviving sources name some of them far less often than rulers.

The artisans and silk weavers seized at Chengdu in 829 show the darkest route by which techniques moved. Forced migration could enlarge a victor’s workshops while breaking families elsewhere. Describing craft “exchange” without this episode would make war look cleaner than it was and erase the people made to carry knowledge.

Zhang Shengwen’s Dali scroll, dated by its colophon to about 1172 to 1175, shows an emperor making offerings amid hundreds of Buddhist figures. Its styles connect Tang and Song China with Tibetan and Southeast Asian traditions. Court artists transformed wide networks into one carefully ordered visual world.

The atlas polygons reach across routes, but a route is not a border. Horses, shells, silver, pilgrims, books and armies could cross places that no ruler controlled tightly. The 800 geometry’s reach toward Luang Prabang should therefore never be defended merely by saying that Nanzhao traded toward Southeast Asia.

sections.title: Health, medicine, clean water and missing toilets

items.text: A Dali book list from 1173 included works on medicine. That proves medical knowledge circulated among literate collectors, but the title list does not reveal the remedies inside, the training of healers or ordinary access to care. No responsible card can turn a court library into a complete public-health system.

Protective Buddhist images and formulas mattered to Nanzhao and Dali patrons, and people may have sought safety through ritual. The sources reviewed here do not let us equate spiritual protection with clinical treatment or name a standard household medicine kit. Religious care and bodily treatment can overlap without being identical.

Channels, embankments and flood control helped fields and settlements manage water. They do not automatically prove safe drinking water, disease prevention or equal access. Agricultural engineering can improve food security while leaving household water questions unanswered, so the evidence supports water management more strongly than sanitation claims.

Wuzhishan’s halls used stone foundations and drains around courtyards. Those drains show builders directing water away from structures, probably including rain and runoff. The excavation report does not identify them as sewage channels, and a temple’s drainage cannot be generalized into a citywide sewer system.

No securely identified Nanzhao or Dali toilet, latrine, cesspit or household waste system appears in the archaeological reports reviewed for this card. That is a limit of the present evidence, not proof that people had no arrangements. We can discuss documented drains; we should leave toilet design unknown.

ending.text: Historical Nanzhao ended when its ruling house was overthrown in 902. Dali began in 937, survived a brief dynastic interruption, and fell to Mongol armies in 1253. Yuan rulers then reused local elites, institutions and religious-political traditions. The atlas’s 1279 cutoff belongs to its imported timeline, not to the death of a people or the fall of “Nan Chao.” Communities around Erhai continued under new governments, carrying forward farms, crafts, kinship, trade and Buddhist institutions while political names and structures changed.
